iGPU: reduce memory overhead, add RAM pressure guard, cap concurrent models, clarify OLLAMA_VULKAN
Problem
Integrated GPUs (iGPU — Intel Iris Xe, AMD APU, etc.) share physical RAM with the CPU. The current Ollama scheduler treats iGPU the same as a discrete GPU in several places, causing:
1. Over-reserved memory overhead — \`MinimumMemory()\` reserves 457 MiB on all non-Metal backends, including iGPU. Since iGPU has no separate VRAM management structures, this wastes headroom that could be used to offload more model layers.
2. No system RAM pressure guard — iGPU \`FreeMemory\` is reported as available VRAM, but this is shared with the OS and CPU processes. Loading a large model can exhaust physical RAM and cause OOM crashes under CPU load.
3. Too many concurrent models by default — \`defaultModelsPerGPU = 3\` allows 3 models loaded simultaneously. On iGPU-only systems this multiplies RAM pressure since all loaded models share the same physical memory pool.
4. Misleading \`OLLAMA_VULKAN\` log — On iGPU-only systems Vulkan is auto-selected, but the server config log shows \`OLLAMA_VULKAN:false\`, making users think Vulkan is not active. There is also no log line explicitly stating which backend was chosen.
Related issues
#13023 — Intel Iris Xe not detected (0 VRAM)
#13029 — Vulkan fails to allocate memory buffer
#12223 — OLLAMA_GPU_OVERHEAD not respected
#13212 — OLLAMA_VULKAN=0 has no effect
#11748 — No shared-memory offload when VRAM full
Proposed fix
\`ml/device.go\`: Return 256 MiB overhead for integrated GPUs (vs 457 MiB for discrete)
\`server/sched.go\`: After \`update

GPU detection silently falls back to CPU when working directory is inaccessible to service user
Description
When `ollama serve` is started as a service user (e.g. `www-data`, `wwwrun`, `nobody`) and the current working directory is not accessible to that user, GPU detection silently fails and ollama falls back to `library=cpu` with no error message or warning.
Steps to Reproduce
# Fails silently → library=cpu
sudo -u www-data bash -c 'cd /root; ollama serve'
# Works → library=cuda
The only difference is the working directory. The environment (PATH, OLLAMA_HOST, CUDA env vars, DISPLAY, XAUTHORITY) is identical.
Environment
OS: openSUSE Tumbleweed (Linux 6.x)
GPU: NVIDIA RTX A3000 12GB (Optimus/PRIME, Dell Precision 7770)
ollama built from source (current main)
Service user: `wwwrun` (equivalent of `www-data`)
Root Cause
The GPU discovery subprocess (the internal `ollama runner --ollama-engine` process spawned by `bootstrapDevices()`) inherits the working directory of the parent process.
During CUDA backend initialization, `libcuda.so` (or a related NVIDIA library) accesses the working directory — most likely to write its JIT kernel cache. If the cwd is a directory the service user cannot access (e.g. `/root` with mode 700), the CUDA backend fails to initialize. Since the discovery subprocess discards stdout/stderr unless `OLLAMA_DEBUG=2` (trace level), this failure is completely invisible to the operator. Ollama then falls back to CPU without any log entry at the default or info log level.

I'd like to propose a small addition to the agent/tooling layer: a built-in `think`
tool in `x/tools` that gives models a structured no-op reasoning step before taking

there doesn't appear to be a built-in reasoning primitive for cases where a model
should explicitly plan before choosing its next tool call.
For local/smaller models, this can help reduce bad tool selection and malformed
arguments by encouraging a plan-first pattern:
1. think
2. choose tool
3. act

Side effects: none

HIP build missing -ffast-math (CUDA has -use_fast_math)
Description
The CUDA backend build uses `-use_fast_math` (ggml-cuda/CMakeLists.txt line 123) but the HIP/ROCm backend does not have the equivalent `-ffast-math` flag. This is a parity gap that leaves performance on the table for all AMD GPU users.
Impact
Benchmarked on an RX 7900 XTX (gfx1100, RDNA3) with ROCm 6.4, using `qwen2.5-coder:14b` (Q4_K_M):
| Benchmark | Without -ffast-math | With -ffast-math | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| code-gen | 60.81 t/s | 64.20 t/s | +5.6% |
| short-explanation | 61.01 t/s | 63.44 t/s | +4.0% |
| list-generation | 61.59 t/s | 63.68 t/s | +3.4% |
This is a free ~4% generation speed improvement for all ROCm users with a one-line change.
Fix
Add to `ml/backend/ggml/ggml/src/ggml-hip/CMakeLists.txt`:
set(CMAKE_HIP_FLAGS "${CMAKE_HIP_FLAGS} -ffast-math")

Transfer-based pulls restart from scratch after interruption, unlike the standard downloader
Hi, I dug through the repo after hitting an interrupted large-model download and found what looks like a real inconsistency in pull behavior.
The standard downloader in `server/download.go` already has resumable behavior built in. It keeps partial state, tracks per-part progress, and resumes with HTTP `Range` requests. That part looks pretty solid.
But the transfer path seems different.
`server/images.go` routes some pulls through `pullWithTransfer(...)`, and `x/imagegen/transfer/transfer.go` explicitly says:
No resume: If a transfer fails, it restarts from scratch.
From `x/imagegen/transfer/download.go`, the current behavior also seems to match that comment:
each blob is downloaded as a whole
data is written to `dest + ".tmp"`
the temp file is removed on failure
retries restart the blob from zero
there is no `Range`-based continuation for partial `.tmp` files
So depending on which pull path gets selected, interrupted downloads can behave very differently:
standard downloader: resumable
transfer downloader: restart from scratch
That makes pull recovery feel inconsistent, especially for larger downloads or unstable connections.
Why this seems worth fixing
For multi-GB model pulls, restarting from zero after a transient interruption is painful in time, bandwidth, and trust. Even if the transfer path was originally optimized for many small blobs, the user-facing behavior still ends up feeling unreliable compared to the standard path.

Ollama incorrectly detects available memory when running in containers
When Ollama runs in a container with a memory limit (this is very important), it incorrectly detects available memory.
When running on bare metal, Ollama uses `MemAvailable` from `/proc/meminfo`. This corresponds to an estimate of how much memory applications have to operate with. Available memory doesn't include the used page cache because page cache can be instantly freed.
When running in a container with a memory limit, Ollama reads the available memory from cgroups. But cgroups don't expose a metric comparable to `MemAvailable` from `/proc/meminfo`. The closest there is is `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current` but that also includes the used page cache. What this means in practice is that after Ollama loads a model once, Linux caches it into page cache and even after the model gets unloaded, the page cache stays filled and since the page cache is included in `memory.current`, Ollama thinks that there isn't enough available memory.
TLDR; `mem.FreeMemory = /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max - /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.current` is too naive and causes Ollama to think it has less memory available than what it has in reality.

PR #15467 added `Function.Index = p.callIndex / p.callIndex++` to `cogito`, `deepseek3`, `functiongemma`, `gemma4`, `lfm2`, `ministral`, `olmo3`, and `qwen3vl`. `qwen3-coder` and `qwen3` already got this in #14484 (2026-02-27).

`ollama ls` takes 5 seconds in interactive terminal (pselect6 timeout on stdout)
Describe the bug
`ollama ls` (and other list/ps commands) consistently takes exactly 5 seconds when run in an interactive terminal (PTY). The same command completes in ~14ms when stdout is piped or not connected to a TTY.
Steps to reproduce
1. Run `time ollama ls` in any interactive terminal (xterm, tmux, gnome-terminal, etc.)
2. Observe ~5 second delay before output appears
Reproducible via `script` which creates a PTY:
# Slow (5s) - with PTY
script -qc 'time ollama ls' /dev/null
# Fast (14ms) - without PTY
Expected behavior
`ollama ls` should complete in milliseconds regardless of terminal type.
Root cause (strace analysis)
`strace -f -T` shows the TUI rendering framework performs a `pselect6` on stdout (fd 1) with a 5-second timeout:
pselect6(2, [1], NULL, NULL, {tv_sec=5, tv_nsec=0}, NULL) = 1 (in [1])       # first call succeeds
pselect6(2, [1], NULL, NULL, {tv_sec=5, tv_nsec=0}, NULL) = 0 (Timeout) <5.005162>  # second call times out
After the 5s timeout, the process proceeds normally:
ioctl(1, TCSETS, ...)  # terminal control
SIGURG                  # Go runtime signal
The 5-second wall time is entirely I/O wait (`user=7ms, sys=14ms, real=5020ms`).
Workaround
Setting `TERM=dumb` bypasses the TUI rendering and eliminates the delay:
TERM=dumb time ollama ls  # 14ms
Alternatively, pipe output: `ollama ls | cat`

create: blobs can still be GC-pruned during long-running create operations after the 1h grace window
PR #15628 reduces the create/GC race by skipping pruning for blobs newer than 1 hour, but the failure mode still exists for create/import flows that run longer than that window.
Right now the protection is still wall-clock based:
`server/images.go` sets `layerPruneGracePeriod = time.Hour`
`PruneLayers()` skips blobs only while `time.Since(info.ModTime()) < layerPruneGracePeriod`
`manifest/layer.go` refreshes mtimes when layers are created or reused, but there is no durable in-progress signal while a long-running create is still active
That means a create flow can still lose pending blobs if:
1. blobs have already been written,
2. the manifest has not been written yet, and
3. another Ollama process runs GC after those blob mtimes age past the 1 hour grace window.
I validated the mechanism locally against current `main` (`57653b8e42d69ec35f68a59857bad4d0f07994a3`) by:
1. creating a blob with `manifest.NewLayer(...)`
2. aging the blob mtime beyond the grace window
3. calling `PruneLayers()`
4. confirming the blob is deleted
5. confirming a later `manifest.NewLayerFromLayer(...)` fails because the blob is gone
Expected behavior: blobs that are still part of an active create/import should not become GC-eligible solely because more than 1 hour elapsed before the manifest was written.
Impact: long-running create/import/quantize flows can still fail late and lose work.

Ollama Issue Draft — hf.co registry host mismatch
Title
Pull from `hf.co/...` fails with "realm host huggingface.co does not match original host hf.co"
Body
Environment
Ollama version: (run `ollama --version`)
OS: macOS 26 (Apple Silicon M3 Max)
Network: Starlink
Command
ollama pull hf.co/ggerganov/whisper.cpp-large-v3:q8_0
Expected
The manifest is fetched and the model is pulled like any other HuggingFace-hosted GGUF.
Actual
pulling manifest
Error: pull model manifest: realm host "huggingface.co" does not match original host "hf.co"
Analysis
The Ollama client accepts `hf.co/*` as a shorthand for HuggingFace. When the backend redirects the manifest realm header to `huggingface.co`, the client refuses because the realm host does not match the originally-requested host. The resolver should treat `hf.co` and `huggingface.co` as the same registry, since `hf.co` is the official short alias.
Workarounds
Install whisper.cpp natively via `brew install whisper-cpp` (not an Ollama model, different runtime).
Try the fully qualified `huggingface.co/ / ` — reportedly sometimes works.
Suggested Fix
In the registry client (likely `server/images.go` or `registry/*.go`), add `hf.co` and `huggingface.co` to an equivalence set so the post-auth realm host check does not trip.
References
Related: issue #10500 (HF 401 Invalid credentials)
Related: issue #13297 (HF token asked despite no auth)
Related: issue #13768 (HF models incorrectly marked no-tools)

Proposal: Local semantic compression for long‑term user memory (accepted by DeepSeek)
Every time a user starts a new chat with an LLM, the model forgets everything about them. The user has to re‑introduce themselves, re‑explain their context, and restate their preferences. This “LLM amnesia” is a real usability problem.
I submitted a proposal to DeepSeek to solve this using local semantic compression. It was accepted as a feature request and added to their backlog.
The core idea
1. Local storage – A folder (for example, `/llm_memory/`) on the user’s device stores short text files – “facts” about the user (e.g., “user name is X”, “prefers concise answers”, “currently working on project Y”).
2. Semantic merging – When the folder reaches a limit (say, 10 files), the system merges semantically similar facts into one instead of deleting old ones.
3. Automatic loading – When a new chat starts, the client sends a compressed profile (last 5‑10 merged facts) to the model inside the system message. The user sees nothing, but the model already knows the relevant context.
4. Privacy by default – No data leaves the user’s device. The server never sees the memory folder, which makes the approach GDPR‑compliant.
Why it matters for local LLMs (Ollama, LM Studio, etc.)
No server‑side storage costs
No privacy risks
Fixed context size (no exponential growth)
Important facts are preserved via merging, not lost via rotation
Where it stands now
The proposal is validated – DeepSeek has already accepted it as a future feature. This is not production code, but a well‑defined architect

rm -rf ~/Desktop/Ollama.app/Contents/_CodeSignature

<plist version="1.0">
<dict>

4. In a terminal, run this command:
otool -l ~/Desktop/Ollama.app/Contents/MacOS/Ollama | grep -A 4 LC_BUILD_VERSION

Summary
Ollama's Vulkan backend hardcodes `{512, 1, 1}` workgroup sizes in dozens of `ggml_vk_create_pipeline(...)` calls and in the corresponding `.comp` shaders (`layout(local_size_x = 512, ...)`). On Raspberry Pi 5 (Broadcom V3D, V3DV driver) the hardware advertises `VkPhysicalDeviceLimits::maxComputeWorkGroupInvocations = 256`, so every one of those pipelines exceeds the device limit and is rejected by the V3D shader compiler:
nir_to_vir.c:  assert(c->local_invocation_index_bits <= 8);
(8 bits = 256 invocations.)
This is the same root cause behind the "Vulkan doesn't work on Raspberry Pi 5" reports against llama.cpp:
`ggml-org/llama.cpp#9801` — "Bug: [vulkan] llama.cpp not work on Raspberry Pi 5"
`ggml-org/llama.cpp#5237` — original Jan 2024 report

`subgroupSize = 16`

OpenAI Compatibility: Support namespace field in tool calls for Responses API parity
The OpenAI "Responses API" (used by tools like Codex CLI) has introduced namespaced tool calling. This allows tools to be grouped (e.g., `mcptilth.search`) and expects a response format that includes a top-level `namespace` field alongside the tool `name`.
Currently, Ollama flattens these into a single `name` string in the `/v1/responses` output. This prevents clients that strictly follow the Responses API (like Codex) from resolving the tool call correctly, as they expect the `namespace` field to be preserved if it was provided in the initial tool spec.

1. Provide a tool definition to Ollama that includes a `namespace` field (or is grouped under a namespace type as seen in the newer Responses API).
2. Have the model call that tool.
3. Observe the output JSON.
4. Actual: `{"tool_calls": [{"function": {"name": "mcpservertool_name", ...}}]}`
5. Expected (for Responses API parity): `{"tool_calls": [{"function": {"name": "tool_name", "namespace": "mcpserver", ...}}]}`

[0.20.5] Runner accepts TCP connection but request never reaches work loop — same shape as resolved-in-0.20.2 #15258
Summary
We hit the same shape as #15258 on Ollama 0.20.5, despite that issue being closed as resolved in 0.20.2 by its reporter. The pattern: large models pinned in memory for hours, then `/api/generate` hangs indefinitely with zero bytes returned, while listing endpoints (`/api/version`, `/api/tags`, `/api/ps`, `/api/embeddings`) keep responding normally.
Forensic analysis (stack samples + lsof) shows this is not a daemon-scheduler issue and not a deadlock primitive — it's a runner-side request-receive failure: the daemon dispatches correctly (TCP ESTABLISHED conn to runner), the runner accepts the connection at the kernel level, but the request payload never reaches the runner's main work loop. The main thread stays in its idle wait-for-work `_pthread_cond_wait` instead of waking to process the inbound request.
Filing this as a probable regression after #15258's 0.20.2 fix (or an adjacent variant the original fix didn't cover). May be related to but distinct from #15923 (which is multi-turn tool-calling crashes — error-emitting, not silent-hang) and #15350 (Gemma 4 Flash Attention hang).

Summary
The Anthropic-compatible endpoint at `/v1/messages` only exposes binary thinking control. There's no way to request the higher-effort modes (`high`, `max`) that the native `/api/chat` endpoint supports for reasoning models like `deepseek-v4-pro:cloud`.

In `anthropic/anthropic.go:375-378`:
var think *api.ThinkValue
if r.Thinking != nil && r.Thinking.Type == "enabled" {
think = &api.ThinkValue{Value: true}
}
`ThinkValue.Value` is hardcoded to `true`, so the request is always equivalent to standard "Thinking" mode regardless of what the client sends. There is no path to `"max"`.

Same prompt (`deepseek-v4-pro:cloud`, math problem requiring reasoning), comparing endpoints:

ollama-engine + SYCL backend silently SIGSEGVs (NULL deref in `ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async`) on hybrid-architecture models — qwen3.5moe, qwen3next, nemotron_h
What happens
When ollama 0.23.0 is built with the GGML SYCL backend (Intel Arc family), and a model whose architecture is on the `OllamaEngineRequired()` list (`qwen35moe`, `qwen3next`, `nemotron_h`, `nemotron_h_moe`, `qwen3vl*`, etc.) is loaded, the runner subprocess crashes with a silent SIGSEGV at `addr=0x0` inside `ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async` on the first prompt request. The model loads successfully and the runner reports `llama runner started in N seconds`; the crash happens at graph compute, not at load.
There is no preceding `Error OP` / `Exception caught` / `unresolved external symbol` line from ggml-sycl, only the bare Go SIGSEGV stack trace, which suggests a NULL function pointer or NULL data pointer is being dereferenced inside the scheduler — most likely a backend interface entry that the new Go-native engine expects ggml-sycl to provide for these models' op set, but which is unimplemented.
Architectures that use the legacy llama.cpp runner (qwen2, qwen3, llama, gemma, glm-4.7, mistral, …) all work correctly via the same SYCL backend.
Reproduction
Hardware: Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage / Xe2, dGPU, 32 GiB).

@ollama/openclaw-web-search: Plugin ships only TypeScript source, no compiled JavaScript
Problem
The npm package `@ollama/openclaw-web-search` (v0.2.2, latest) only ships `index.ts` (TypeScript source) but no compiled JavaScript entry point. OpenClaw's plugin loader cannot load TypeScript directly — it looks for one of:
./dist/index.js
./dist/index.mjs
./dist/index.cjs
index.js
None of these exist. This causes the plugin to fail to load entirely, logged as:
plugin openclaw-web-search: installed plugin package requires compiled runtime output for TypeScript entry index.ts
plugin not found: openclaw-web-search (stale config entry ignored)
Root Cause
`package.json` declares `"main": "index.ts"` but only includes `index.ts` in the `"files"` array, with no compiled JavaScript artifact.
There is no `prepublishOnly`, `build`, or `postinstall` script to compile the TypeScript to JavaScript.
Expected Behavior
The npm package should include a compiled JavaScript entry point (e.g., `index.js` or `dist/index.js`) so that OpenClaw can load the plugin without requiring a manual build step.
Workaround
Users can manually compile with esbuild:
cd ~/.openclaw/extensions/openclaw-web-search && npx esbuild index.ts --bundle --format=esm --platform=node --outfile=index.js
But this is wiped on every update/reinstall.
Suggested Fix
Either:
1. Add a `prepublishOnly` / `build` script in `package.json` that compiles `index.ts` → `index.js` (or `dist/index.js`)
2. Or ship the compiled JavaScript directly in the npm package
Environment
`@ollama/openclaw-web-search` v0.2.2

app/ui: chat shows loading flash when switching between conversations
When switching from one chat to another, there's a brief "Loading chat..." flash before the messages appear. This happens every time, even if the chat data was already fetched.
Why it happens
The route loader for the chat page fires off a data prefetch but doesn't wait for it to complete. The component mounts immediately, finds no data in the cache yet, and renders the loading state for a split second until the data arrives.
Expected behavior
The router should wait for the chat data to be ready before mounting the component, so the user sees the messages instantly without any loading flash.

app/ui: chat doesn't scroll to the bottom on page refresh or when switching conversations
When you open a long chat via a direct link or refresh the page, the chat stays scrolled to the top instead of jumping to the most recent messages at the bottom. The same can happen intermittently when switching between chats — sometimes the scroll-to-bottom just doesn't fire.
Why it happens
The scroll-to-bottom logic tracks the previous chat ID to detect navigation. Two problems:
1. On page refresh, the tracking ref is initialized with the current chat ID, so the "did the chat change?" check immediately fails — it thinks you're already on this chat.
2. The ref gets updated unconditionally on every render, even before messages have actually loaded. So when messages finally arrive and the effect re-runs, it thinks nothing changed because the ref was already set.
Expected behavior
Opening any existing chat — whether via navigation or page refresh — should always scroll to the most recent messages at the bottom.

app/ui: centralize theme detection and tokenize only the active theme in code blocks
Every code block in a chat message runs syntax highlighting twice — once for light mode and once for dark mode. Both results are rendered as two separate ` ` elements, and CSS hides the inactive one. On a chat with hundreds of code blocks, this doubles the Shiki processing time for no visible benefit.
There's also no centralized way to know which theme is currently active. The theme names are hardcoded as string literals scattered across files.
Why it matters
Shiki's TextMate grammar regex is the single most expensive operation during chat loading. Cutting it in half by only tokenizing the active theme has a massive impact.

app/ui: thinking section re-creates ResizeObserver on every token and renders markdown when hidden
Two problems in the thinking/reasoning panel:
1. While the model is actively thinking, the ResizeObserver that measures content height is torn down and re-created on every single streamed token. This is unnecessary overhead — a ResizeObserver automatically detects size changes once attached.
2. When thinking is finished and the section is collapsed, the full Streamdown + Shiki markdown rendering still runs behind the scenes even though the content is completely hidden (opacity 0, height 0). This wastes CPU cycles on invisible content.
Expected behavior
The ResizeObserver should be set up once when the element mounts and left running. The markdown rendering should be skipped entirely when the thinking section is collapsed and finished.

app/ui: unnecessary JSON re-parsing and missing memo dependencies in message components
Several small performance issues across the message rendering pipeline add up, especially in chats with many tool calls:
1. Tool call arguments are re-parsed on every render — `BrowserToolCallDisplay` calls `JSON.parse` on tool call arguments during render without memoizing the result. Every re-render (e.g., during streaming) re-parses the same JSON.
2. Collapsed tool results still run JSON.stringify — When a tool result is collapsed and invisible, the component still stringifies the raw JSON on every render. This should be deferred until the user actually expands the section.
3. Message memo comparator is missing `lastToolQuery` — The custom `React.memo` comparator for the `Message` component doesn't include `lastToolQuery` in the comparison, which can cause missed memoization opportunities or stale renders.
4. `lastToolQueries` recalculates on every streaming token — The memoized computation depends on the full `messages` array reference, which changes on every streamed token. Using `messages.length` as the dependency would prevent unnecessary recalculations since tool queries only change when new messages are added.
5. Unreachable code after early returns — In `ToolCallDisplay`, there's a code path that checks for `browser.*` tool names that can never be reached because a previous branch already handles all non-`browser.*` names and returns.
6. `browserToolResult` prop is untyped — The prop is typed as `any` in `MessageList` instead of using the existing `BrowserToolResult

server: stabilize TestSchedExpireRunner timeout
The `TestSchedExpireRunner` test is frequently flaky in CI environments, especially on Windows and macOS runners. The test fails with the error message `expected model to be unloaded`, which indicates that a model remains in the scheduler's memory instead of being correctly expired and unloaded.
Technical Analysis
The issue is caused by a very aggressive context timeout of `20ms` used in the test setup. In virtualized CI environments, the time needed to initialize the scheduler and process the asynchronous model unloading often exceeds this narrow window.
Logs from failed CI runs show the following debug message:
`level=DEBUG msg="shutting down scheduler completed loop"`
This confirms that the scheduler's background loop is exiting prematurely because the context has timed out. When the loop shuts down too early, it misses the signal to process the finished request and unload the model. As a result, the model stays in the internal "loaded" map, causing the test's final assertion to fail.
Example of failure:

Fuse Qwen3Next Gated Delta Net autoregressive decode
Qwen3Next and Qwen35 use Gated Delta Net recurrent layers. In autoregressive decode, the current graph expands this recurrent update into many smaller tensor operations. llama.cpp has since added a fused `ggml_gated_delta_net` op for this path.
This issue proposes bringing that fused autoregressive decode path into Ollama while keeping behaviour unchanged for unsupported backends.
Proposed shape:
Backport the upstream ggml Gated Delta Net op from llama.cpp while Ollama's pinned llama.cpp commit predates that implementation.
Use the fused op only for autoregressive decode.
Keep chunked prefill on the existing explicit graph.
Gate the fused path by backend capability, so unsupported backends continue to use the existing path rather than silently falling back to CPU.
Add CPU reference tests, CUDA parity tests for supported head dimensions, and multi-step recurrent state tests.
The change should not add a user-facing option. It is an internal execution optimisation for existing Qwen3Next and Qwen35 models.
Validation expected before merge:
ggml CPU reference parity.
CUDA versus CPU parity for supported `S_v` values.
Multi-step recurrent state continuity.
Native `ggml`, `ggml-cpu` and `ggml-cuda` builds.
End-to-end smoke or benchmark evidence on a Qwen3Next or Qwen35 GGUF.

PushHandler can panic with nil pointer on `spinner.Stop()`
Found this while poking around `cmd/cmd.go` to understand the push flow.
What's happening
`PushHandler` declares `spinner` as nil at line 948:
var spinner *progress.Spinner  // nil
The only place it ever gets assigned is inside the progress callback `fn` (line 974), and only when the server sends a response with an empty `Digest`:
} else if status != resp.Status {
...
spinner = progress.NewSpinner(status)  // <-- only assignment
}
So if the server only sends blob-digest responses (all with non-empty `Digest`), `spinner` stays nil the whole time.
The error path at line 983-985 handles this:
if err := client.Push(cmd.Context(), &request, fn); err != nil {
if spinner != nil { spinner.Stop() }  // <-- guarded
...
}
But the success path right after it doesn't:
p.Stop()
spinner.Stop()  // <-- no nil check, will panic if nil
`PullHandler` (line 1417) doesn't call `spinner.Stop()` at all on success, which makes this look like an oversight rather than intentional.
Is it reachable right now?
Honestly, probably not in production. The server (`PushModel` in `server/images.go:531`) starts with `{Status: "retrieving manifest"}` which creates the spinner. So in practice there's always at least one status-only response.
But the guard should be there anyway — the error path has it, and there's nothing in the contract guaranteeing the server always sends a status response first.

The backend model reference parser recognizes explicit source tags like `gpt-oss:20b:cloud` or legacy tag suffixes like `gpt-oss:20b-cloud`. It does not recognize `gpt-oss:20bcloud`, so subsequent requests use an invalid or nonexistent local model instead of cloud.

Feature request: add 'agy' (Antigravity CLI) to ollama launch integrations
What is agy?
Antigravity CLI (`agy`) is Google's AI CLI tool. It's a terminal-based AI coding assistant similar to Claude Code, built into the Antigravity ecosystem (Google's AI IDE). It's installed via `brew install antigravity-cli` and used as `agy` in the terminal.
Current state
`ollama launch` supports many integrations (claude, codex, openclaw, vscode, etc.) but not `agy`:
ollama launch claude --model deepseek-v4-pro:cloud   ✅ works
ollama launch agy    --model deepseek-v4-pro:cloud   ❌ not supported
Why it matters
As ollama cloud models grow in popularity, users want to use them across ALL their AI tools — not just Claude Code. Antigravity CLI is becoming a common tool (especially for those in the Google/Antigravity ecosystem), and the gap forces users to choose between ollama models and the agy workflow.
Technical note
Unlike Claude Code (which respects `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` env vars), agy routes through Google's cloud API (`daily-cloudcode-pa.googleapis.com`). A simple env-var proxy approach may not work out of the box. The integration might need to be explored with the Antigravity team to understand what model override mechanisms are available.
Relevant: agy's model selection appears to be managed server-side at Google. The Antigravity IDE (desktop app) has UI for custom endpoints/configs, but the CLI (`agy`) does not expose these directly.

In the new llama.cpp native runner architecture, there is an issue with memory/VRAM reclamation during single-user, long-context scenarios (128K window).
The ~25GB KV Cache is not released when a session ends or a "New Conversation" is triggered in the upstream app (Dify/RAGFlow). Instead, it remains locked in VRAM (stuck at ~80GB total allocation).
Crucially, the exact moment the upstream Reranker service (managed by Xinference) is restarted—which forces a physical TCP connection closure—Ollama immediately and cleanly flushes the 25GB KV Cache, dropping the VRAM back down to the model's static weight level (~55GB).
This indicates that the new `llama.cpp` runner heavily relies on absolute TCP connection teardown to flush the context cache, causing unexpected memory degradation when upstream API gateways/microservices keep the HTTP connection alive.
1. Spin up a full RAG stack via Docker: Dify + RAGFlow + Xinference (Reranker) + Ollama (v0.30.0 Pre-release).

4. Click "New Conversation" in Dify/RAGFlow to end the session. The 25GB KV Cache is unpredictably retained in VRAM and does not release after several minutes.
5. Manually run `docker restart `.

nemotron3 library models ship no sampling parameters, running at engine defaults instead of NVIDIA's recommended profile
What
The `nemotron3:33b` library model ships an empty Modelfile PARAMETER block, so it runs at Ollama engine defaults (`temperature 0.8`, `top_p 0.9`, `repeat_penalty 1.1`). NVIDIA's model card recommends `temperature 0.6` / `top_p 0.95` for reasoning mode and recommends leaving penalties unset.
$ curl -s localhost:11434/api/show -d '{"model":"nemotron3:33b"}' | jq -r '.parameters'
null
Sibling library models ship their vendors' recommended sampling profiles:
gemma4:26b       → temperature 1, top_k 64, top_p 0.95
qwen3.6:35b-a3b  → temperature 1, top_k 20, top_p 0.95, min_p 0, presence_penalty 1.5, repeat_penalty 1
References: NVIDIA model card, ollama.com/library/nemotron3
Why
Reasoning mode is the model's default, so out of the box users sample at settings that match none of NVIDIA's documented modes (thinking: 0.6/0.95; instruct: 0.2/greedy). In an A/B on the same coding prompt (thinking on, q4_K_M, Apple M4 Pro), engine defaults produced ~45% more reasoning tokens and ~28% higher wall-clock than the vendor profile, with the same answer quality (single run, directional).
How
Add `PARAMETER temperature 0.6` and `PARAMETER top_p 0.95` to the `nemotron3` library Modelfiles, matching the convention already used for `gemma4` and `qwen3.6`
Consider `PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.0` so the engine default of 1.1 does not apply, per NVIDIA's guidance to leave penalties off
Environment: Ollama server 0.30.5 / client 0.30.7, macOS (Apple Silicon), `nemotron3:33b` (q4_K_M).

Bug: `extractFileNames` fractures file paths when parent directories contain valid file extensions
Description
The file path extractor tokenizer in cmd/interactive.go fractures a single continuous, valid path sequence into multiple token fragments if an intermediate parent directory name contains an identical file extension string (e.g., .png, .jpg).
Root Cause Analysis
In extractFileNames, the regex pattern uses a lazy evaluation quantifier +? leading directly into the extension match:
regexPattern := `(?:[a-zA-Z]:)?(?:\./|/|\\)[\S\\ ]+?\.(?i:jpg|jpeg|png|webp|wav)\b`
Because the engine seeks the shortest possible match that fulfills the expression, it stops evaluating as soon as it satisfies the first occurrence of a valid extension word boundary. It fails an extensional path monotonicity invariance check by treating an internal subpath directory name as a terminal file target.
Steps to Reproduce
Pass a string containing a nested path where a folder mimics a file:
package main
import (
"fmt"
Expected Behavior
The function evaluates the string monolithically and returns a single complete token slice:
[]string{"./image.png/image.png"}
Actual Behavior
The evaluation yields a fractured slice consisting of an incomplete subpath string and a trailing fragment:
[]string{"./image.png/", "/image.png"}
Remediation
PR fix will be opened imminently

x/mlxrunner: gemma-4 MLX models fail to load or decode (quant, KV-sharing, BOS)
MLX-only support for running the gemma-4 family (e4b / 12B, instruct + base) from mlx-community safetensors. Draft for maintainer feedback per CONTRIBUTING (issue-first).
Scope
MLX runner / safetensors only (e.g. `mlx-community/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-4bit`, `mlx-community/gemma-4-12B-it-qat-4bit`, `mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-4bit`).
GGUF + llama.cpp not covered.
Symptoms
Three independent issues currently prevent these checkpoints from working:
1. Mixed-precision QAT crashes at decode. QAT checkpoints pack attention at 4-bit and the MLP at 8-bit, but the container metadata declares a single global affine quant type. The loader reads the 8-bit MLP as 4-bit and `QuantizedMatmul` produces an invalid result.
2. `num_kv_shared_layers` checkpoints fail to load. KV-shared layers reuse a donor layer's K/V and carry only `q_proj`/`q_norm`/`o_proj` (no `k_proj`/`v_proj`/`k_norm`). The loader unconditionally requires the k/v projections.
3. Completion/raw output is degenerate. No BOS is prepended when `tokenizer_config.json` omits `add_bos_token`, and gemma is highly BOS-sensitive (verified: the same weights run coherently in `mlx_lm` with BOS, garbage without).
Proposed fix
quant: infer per-tensor bit width from the packed weight/scale shapes when the container metadata is inconsistent.
gemma4: skip the k/v-projection validation for KV-shared layers (the forward already sources K/V from the donor).
tokenizer: honor the `tokenizer.json` post-processor BOS when `add_bos_token` is absent; dedu

Add support for ppc64le architecture
Current State:
Currently, Ollama officially supports common architectures (amd64, arm64), but the ppc64le (IBM Power) architecture lacks build support. Users on PowerPC systems are currently forced to use manual patches / community-provided binaries, which complicates adoption and maintenance for enterprise AI users.
Proposed Feature:
I would like to propose officially adding ppc64le as a supported architecture for Ollama.
Technical Context:
The underlying inference engine, llama.cpp, has robust and mature support for ppc64le.
I have verified that by updating the llama.cpp submodule to version b9692, Ollama builds and runs seamlessly on ppc64le (POWER9/Power10) systems. Supporting this architecture requires no changes to the core Ollama codebase, just updating the LLAMA_CPP_VERSION to b9692 is sufficient.
Benefits:

With `devstral-small-2` (architecture `mistral3`), if a tool's function has a parameter named exactly `name`, the model's tool call is silently dropped: the API returns empty `content`, `finish_reason: "stop"`, and no `tool_calls` - even though `completion_tokens > 0` (the model *did* generate a tool call). Renaming the parameter to anything else fixes it. Only the exact lowercase `name` triggers the bug.
This breaks agent frameworks that expose tools such as `skill_view(name=...)`, `get_item(name=...)`, etc.: every call to those tools comes back empty.
Minimal reproduction
Fails (parameter named `name`):
curl -s http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
"model": "devstral-small-2",
"stream": false,
→ `choices[0].message.content == ""`, `finish_reason == "stop"`, no `tool_calls` (with `completion_tokens` ≈ 13–15).
Works (same request, parameter renamed `query`):
curl -s http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
"model": "devstral-small-2",
"stream": false,
→ proper `tool_calls`: `foo({"query":"bar"})`, `finish_reason == "tool_calls"`.
Tested parameter keys: `query`, `Name`, `names`, `skill_name`, `arguments`, `nom` → all work. Only the exact lowercase `name` → empty. Same behaviour with `stream: true`.
This is NOT the known "streaming breaks tool calling" issue. The repro above uses `stream: false` and still fails. The trigger is solely the parameter key `name`, independent of streaming.

server: malformed registry WWW-Authenticate header panics getValue (slice OOB / DoS)
When ollama pulls from a registry that returns a 401 with a malformed `WWW-Authenticate` header, the challenge parser slices out of range and panics.
Where
`server/images.go`, `getValue` (called by `parseRegistryChallenge`):
func getValue(header, key string) string {
startIdx := strings.Index(header, key+"=")
if startIdx == -1 { return "" }
startIdx += len(key) + 2          // assumes key="..." — skips key, '=', and an opening quote
The `+2` assumes the value is quoted (`key="..."`). For an unquoted/empty value such as `realm=` at the end of the header, `startIdx` is advanced past the end of the string and `header[startIdx:endIdx]` panics.
Impact
Denial of service. A malicious or compromised registry (or an on-path attacker on a non-TLS pull) returns `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm=` and crashes the ollama process performing the pull. Crash/DoS, not memory corruption.
Reproduce
`parseRegistryChallenge("Bearer realm=")`. Confirmed on current `main` (`964ea42`, 2026-07-03):
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:7] with length 6
Suggested fix
Bounds-check `startIdx` against `len(header)` before slicing and handle the unquoted/empty-value case; return `""` on a malformed header instead of panicking. Proposed in an accompanying PR.
Disclosure
Reported to `hello@ollama.com` on 2026-05-13, no response; filing here for visibility and tracking. Happy to coordinate on the fix.

template: unbounded {{range N}} in a model template hangs Execute (DoS)
A malicious model TEMPLATE containing a large integer range causes template rendering to loop effectively without bound, hanging the request.
Where
`template/template.go`, `Execute` → Go `text/template` integer `range` (Go 1.22+).
A template such as:
{{range 100000000000}}{{end}}
parses successfully and, on `Execute`, iterates 1e11 times. On current `main` (`964ea42`, 2026-07-03), `Execute` did not return within 8 seconds (the loop is CPU-bound and unbounded from the caller's side).
Impact
Denial of service. A model whose template is attacker-influenced (a pulled/created model) hangs whichever request renders it. Uncontrolled resource consumption (CWE-400); no memory corruption.
Reproduce
Parse and execute the template above with any non-empty `Values` (e.g. `Values{Prompt: "x", Suffix: "y"}`).
Suggested approach (design)
Unlike the parser panics, this has no clean one-line fix — a running `text/template` `Execute` can't be cleanly interrupted, and output-size limits miss the empty-body case. Reasonable options:
Parse-time validation: reject or cap a static integer-range bound above a threshold when parsing a model template.
Render budget: execute model-supplied templates against an iteration/work cap.
Both are design choices, so I'm filing this as an issue for discussion rather than a PR. Happy to implement whichever direction you prefer.
Disclosure
Reported to `hello@ollama.com` on 2026-05-11, no response; filing here for visibility and tracking.

Resolve all blobs referenced by the selected model.
Copy only the required files.
Preserve the manifest and metadata needed for importing.
Produce a portable directory that can be transferred to another machine.
On the destination machine, users could simply run something like:
ollama import /mnt/export/llama3.1-8b
or
ollama copy --import /mnt/export/llama3.1-8b

What happened

Three fields read directly from the file are used unchecked:

3. Inverted / out-of-range offsets — `Offsets[1] < Offsets[0]` yields a negative tensor `size`, which panics in the `make([]T, size/n)` calls in `WriteTo`.
Because conversion runs in a goroutine without `recover`, the panic isn't contained to the request.

A crafted (or corrupted) safetensors file passed through conversion crashes the process instead of returning an error. This is a robustness/availability issue on the model-import path.

Malformed safetensors input should be rejected with an error, consistent with how the GGUF readers (`fs/ggml`, `fs/gguf`) bound every length, count, and offset (`checkedLength`, `MaxArraySize`, file-size checks).

What happened?
`convert/convert_deepseek2.go:127` in `deepseek2Model.Tensors` has an integer overflow that leads to an out of bounds slice write.

for i := range p.HiddenLayers {

merges[i*3+1] = merge{...}
`p.HiddenLayers` is a `uint32` populated directly from the attacker controlled `num_hidden_layers` field in the model's `config.json`, with no bounds check. `p.HiddenLayers*3` is computed as `uint32` arithmetic and silently wraps around. The conversion runs inside a background goroutine started by `server.(*Server).CreateHandler` at `server/create.go:119` with no `defer recover()`. replied:

useful. Ideally, support would be added for both runners.
This issue proposes that Ollama-native design — scheduler-owned prefill/KV cache reuse across model reloads, with no new public API, implemented for both runners.
Problem
With a local LLM, an agentic workflow typically prepends the same large system prompt (rules, tool definitions) on every turn.
Ollama already reuses the in-memory prefix cache while the model stays loaded, so consecutive turns are fast. But that reuse only lives as long as the runner: when the model is unloaded — keep-alive expiry (5 minutes by default) or a model switch — the state is gone, and the next request recomputes the full prefill, paying a TTFT cost that grows with prompt length — ~440 ms at ~3.8K tokens, ~7 s at ~31K (llama3.2:3b, RTX 4070).
In practice this means TTFT varies by orders of magnitude *within the same session*, depending only on whether an unload happened in between.
Users who aren't aware of the keep-alive behavior can easily mistake this variance for a performance bug.
Proposal
Scheduler-owned, no new public API. The scheduler saves the prefill
cache right before a runner shuts down and restores it after the same
model+options combination is loaded again, entirely inside one daemon
process. Nothing new is exposed on the API.
Both runners, runner-agnostic interface. llama-server reuses the bundled

Bare-JSON tool call models: content generated after a tool call is silently dropped
For models whose template has no text tool-call tag (the tools parser falls back to the `{` or `[` tag and treats bare JSON as a tool call), any content the model generates after a tool call is silently dropped, and the parser never leaves tool-calling state.
Example, using the parser the way the server streams into it:
p := tools.NewParserWithTag(myTools, "{")
calls, content := p.Add(`{"name": "get_temperature", "arguments": {"city": "Tokyo"}}`)
// calls: 1, content: "" (correct)
_, content = p.Add(" I called the tool for you.")
The trailing text is buffered forever, and at the end of the stream `Content()` returns `""` because a tool call was parsed. The client receives the tool call but none of the text the model generated after it, with no indication anything was lost.
Cause
Two things in `tools/tools.go` combine:
1. `parseToolCall` advances the buffer with `p.buffer = p.buffer[end:]`, where `end` is the index of the closing brace returned by `findArguments`. The closing `}` of the parsed call is left at the front of the buffer.
2. `done()` decides completion by brace counting from the current buffer. The leftover `}` immediately drives the count negative, so it can never reach zero again and the parser stays in tool-calling state for the rest of the stream.
The same applies to the `[` tag after the list closes.

systemctl mask ollama fails ("File already exists"), installer writes the unit into /etc/systemd/system
On Linux, `install.sh` writes the systemd unit directly into `/etc/systemd/system/ollama.service` - the administrator *override* namespace, and the highest-precedence directory on systemd's unit search path. Because a real unit file already occupies that exact path, there is no supported way to keep the service permanently off:
`systemctl mask ollama` fails - mask needs to place its `/dev/null` symlink at `/etc/systemd/system/ollama.service`, but the installer's regular file is already there.
`systemctl disable ollama` does not survive a reinstall/upgrade - re-running `install.sh` unconditionally calls `systemctl enable ollama` and restarts it, silently undoing the admin's decision.
The net effect: an administrator who deliberately turned the service off has no first-class, durable way to make that stick. The only workaround is to manually relocate the unit out of `/etc` first (`mv` to `/usr/local/lib/systemd/system/`) before masking - i.e. to put the unit where it should have been installed in the first place.
# 1) Install
$ curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh
# 2) Try to permanently prevent the service from starting
Minimal, ollama-independent reproduction of the mask failure (any regular unit file placed in `/etc/systemd/system` behaves identically):
$ printf '[Unit]\nDescription=x\n[Service]\nExecStart=/bin/true\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/masktest.service >/dev/null
$ sudo systemctl mask masktest
Failed to mask unit: File '/etc/systemd/system/masktest.ser

Feature request: let MoE experts live in host RAM with on-demand GPU compute — run 16B/35B MoE on 8GB GPUs without OOM
TL;DR
Ollama currently inherits llama.cpp's default: all MoE expert weights get loaded into VRAM. That's why a 16B MoE model (6GB file) needs 23GB VRAM, and 8GB/12GB GPUs OOM on models that *should* fit. MoE experts are only activated sparsely (2-8 of 256 per token) — the full weight set doesn't need to sit on the GPU.
I've built and measured a working approach: keep expert weights in host RAM (pinned), let cuBLAS DMA-read them over PCIe on demand, and let VRAM hold only non-expert layers + KV cache. Real measurements (RTX 4090, custom llama.cpp fork):
| Model | Standard (all-in-VRAM) | Host-RAM experts | VRAM saved | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite Q2_K (16B MoE, 6GB file) | 23.3GB VRAM, 65 t/s | 1.6GB VRAM, 37.5 t/s | −93% | 58% retained |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (35B MoE, 11GB file) | OOM on 8GB cards | 2.1GB VRAM, 46.8 t/s | — | ≈ parity |
| Qwen3-235B-A22B Q2_K (81.7GB) | impossible on consumer GPUs | ~8GB VRAM (target) | — | TBD |

Ollama's user base is overwhelmingly consumer GPUs — 8GB, 12GB, 16GB cards. The single most common complaint in "ollama OOM" threads is: *model file is small but it won't load*. For MoE models the file size lies — the VRAM requirement is 3-4x the file.

Laguna parser turns JSON in ordinary content into a tool call, aborting or corrupting the reply
Summary
The Laguna parser (`poolside-v1`, `model/parsers/laguna.go`) scans streamed content for tool calls the model may emit as bare JSON objects, with no ` ` tags around them. That scan is needed, but its detection rule accepts any JSON object in the reply, including one the model wrote as part of an answer. The scan runs whenever the request declares tools, so a reply that quotes JSON, such as a config example or an API response, fails in one of four ways:
1. The request aborts with `{"error":"empty Laguna tool call name"}` and everything generated so far is lost.
2. The parser withholds all content from the object onward and delivers it in one block in the final message, so streaming stops mid-reply.
3. An object containing a `name` field becomes a tool call to a tool that was never declared, and the client receives no content.
4. A tool call with an empty name is attached to a streamed message that also carries content.
The parser examines its buffer only at the end of each chunk, so token boundaries decide which of the four failures occurs. A single generation can produce more than one of them.

mlxrunner: requests are serialized; support batched/concurrent decode
The experimental MLX runner (`x/mlxrunner`) handles one request at a time. Concurrent API calls are queued and run one by one:
`runner.go`: a single goroutine consumes the unbuffered `Requests` channel, so the next request only starts after the current one finishes.
`pipeline.go`: `const pipelineSlot = 0` with the comment "The runner serializes requests today so we just use a fixed slot ID."
`server/sched.go`: `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL` is only applied on the llama.cpp path. The MLX path (`IsMLX`) never receives `numParallel`, so the setting has no effect for MLX models.
Why it matters
Single-token decode is memory-bandwidth bound. With batched decode, B requests share one read of the weights per step, so total throughput scales well until compute becomes the limit. Measured on an M4 Pro with a 16B MoE (mxfp8, ~1.1 GB weight reads per token): decode runs at ~105 tok/s for one request, and the dense part of the reads (attention, lm_head, shared experts) would amortize fully across a batch. A rough estimate for B=4 is 2.5-3x total throughput.
What already exists
Parts of the runner look batch-ready:
`batch.Batch` carries per-sequence `SeqOffsets` / `SeqQueryLens`.
The sampler is slot-based ("batched, slot-based sampler", multiple slots supported).
What is missing
A decode loop that collects active sequences and builds one batch per step (continuous batching), instead of one pipeline per request.

the OpenAI API supports a concept called 'custom tools'
Custom tools work in much the same way as JSON schema-driven function tools. But rather than providing the model explicit instructions on what input your tool requires, the model can pass an arbitrary string back to your tool as input. This is useful to avoid unnecessarily wrapping a response in JSON, or to apply a custom grammar to the response (more on this below).
afaiu one advantage of it is that some models have an easier time giving correct output when they don't also have to nest it in JSON (think of shell commands that compose multiple cli tools and python in one 'sh' tool call)

Proposal: add a KV connector framework for pluggable external KV cache backends
Summary
I'd like to propose a small-but-extensible KV connector framework in Ollama so that external KV cache systems can be integrated incrementally. Long term this could enable LMCache and similar systems, but the scope of this issue is intentionally smaller:
1. add the framework and lifecycle hooks
2. ship a simple `ExampleConnector`
3. have `ExampleConnector` persist KV/prefix-cache state to local files only
Why now
Ollama already has most of the pieces needed for this on the MLX path:
`llm.LlamaServer` is the backend boundary
`server/sched.go` owns model/runner selection and request lifecycle
`x/mlxrunner/cache.Cache`, `x/mlxrunner/cache.Snapshot`, and `x/mlxrunner/prefix_cache.go` already model restorable cache state, snapshots, and prefix matching
What is missing is a pluggable boundary between request lifecycle and where cache state lives.
Prior art / reference
vLLM's KV connector design is a useful reference point:
`vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/base.py`
the example connector layered on top of it
the LMCache connector layered on top of it
I do not think Ollama should copy the vLLM API 1:1. vLLM needs separate scheduler-side and worker-side primitives because it is coordinating distributed executors and per-layer load/save.
Ollama's first implementation can be simpler because request scheduling and cache ownership are local and serialized in the MLX runner.

add a backend-agnostic connector interface at the runner layer

We ran into this while trying to reproduce a result we had from `llama4` in Ollama by running the same model directly in llama.cpp, using unsloth's Q4_K_M weights (Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-GGUF, file `Q4_K_M/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-Q4_K_M-00001-of-00002.gguf`). For identical prompts, Ollama reported noticeably more tokens than llama.cpp, around 8-10% more. Tokenization is deterministic and doesn't depend on the weights, so for the same model the two should produce the same tokens.
It comes down to the pre-tokenizer. The model Ollama ships (`ollama pull llama4`) has:
tokenizer.ggml.pre = default
while the unsloth GGUF we were using has:
tokenizer.ggml.pre = llama4
(this is also what llama.cpp's own `convert_hf_to_gguf.py` writes for Llama 4.)
With `default`, llama.cpp uses its GPT-2 fallback pre-tokenizer regex instead of the Llama 4 one. Same vocabulary and merges, but the text gets split differently, so the token IDs don't match.
The cause is in the converter. `convert/tokenizer.go` identifies the pre-tokenizer by hashing its `Split` regex(es) and matching a fixed list of digests. Problem
`cmd/internal/fileutil.WriteWithBackup` names backups using Unix timestamps with one-second resolution:
backupPath := filepath.Join(dir, fmt.Sprintf("%s.%d", name, time.Now().Unix()))
When the same file is written more than once within a second, each write selects the same backup path. A later backup overwrites the earlier one, potentially replacing the true pre-change state with an intermediate configuration.

Identified with:
Expected behavior
Every content-changing write creates a distinct backup.
The earliest backup preserves the exact state from before the first write.
Existing pruning continues to retain the configured number of newest backups.
Possible approach
Use a collision-resistant suffix, such as nanoseconds or a uniquely created backup filename, while keeping ordering and pruning deterministic.
Test coverage

1. The exact original content remains in a backup.
2. Intermediate versions do not overwrite earlier backups.
3. The final target contains the latest content.
4. Retention still keeps only the newest configured number of backups.

Qwen3.8-27B MTP variants are 2x slower than non-MTP on Apple Silicon - is this expected?
I measured the MTP variants of Qwen3.8-27B as consistently slower than the same quantization without MTP heads, on Apple Silicon. I do not know whether this is expected behaviour for the speculative path on Metal or a defect. Below is what I measured, with a negative control and a reproduction recipe.
Measurements
Two prompts, 200 tokens each, `temperature: 0`, three repetitions, machine quiet. The idea: if an engine performs speculative decoding, predictable content generates faster than unpredictable content, because several tokens are validated per weight read.
engine              MTP heads   predictable   unpredictable   ratio
------------------  ---------   -----------   -------------   -----
GGUF q4_K_M         no          11.91 tok/s     11.78 tok/s   1.01x
GGUF mtp-q4_K_M     yes         11.40 tok/s      5.14 tok/s   2.22x
The first row is the negative control: no MTP heads, therefore no possible content-dependence. It is flat, which is what tells us the protocol is measuring speculation and not word length or vocabulary size.
Interpretation
Taking `q4_K_M` without heads as the baseline (11.78 tok/s, the cost of a token with no speculation):
When drafts are rejected, `mtp-q4_K_M` falls to 5.14 tok/s, i.e. 2.3x slower than no speculation at all. The draft alone therefore costs slightly more than a full pass.
When drafts are accepted, it climbs back to 11.40 tok/s, i.e. barely the no-heads baseline.

[Vulkan Multi-GPU] VRAM Accounting Desync
Title
[Vulkan Multi-GPU] VRAM Accounting Desync: Scheduler sees 15GB free, llama-server sees 1.1GB, forcing unnecessary CPU fallback
Environment
Ollama Version: 0.32.13
OS: Linux Fedora 43
Hardware: 4x AMD Radeon Instinct (4x 32GB = 128GB total VRAM)
Backend: Vulkan (RADV)
Issue Description
There is a significant desync in VRAM accounting between the Go scheduler and the C++ `llama-server` subprocess when running multiple models on the Vulkan backend.
When a small LLM model (`qwen3.8:27b-384k`) is already loaded, the Go scheduler correctly calculates that there is still ~12-15 GB of free VRAM per GPU. It attempts to load a small secondary embedding model (`E5-large:fp32`, ~2.3 GB) and assigns it to a single GPU.
However, the `llama-server` Vulkan subprocess reads a massive amount of `unaccounted` memory (likely due to Vulkan driver memory pools/fragmentation from the first model). It sees only `1174 MiB` free, fails to fit the 2.3 GB model, and falls back to CPU execution.
Result: A tiny 2.3GB embedding model falls back to `CPU_Mapped` execution, despite having ~50GB of total theoretical VRAM free across the 4-GPU cluster.
$ ollama ps
NAME                ID              SIZE      PROCESSOR         CONTEXT    UNTIL
E5-large:fp32       86c2febe757e    2.3 GB    96%/4% CPU/GPU    512        Forever
qwen3.8:27b-384k    d7f5f0ce4759    80 GB     100% GPU          393216     Forever
$ rocm-smi
============================================ ROCm System Management Interface ===========

There should be a default disabled thinking environment variable.
Ollama users are primarily personal desktop versions, with a significant share. For individuals, generation speed is more critical than quality. On ordinary personal computers, the thinking mode shows some effect but has limited impact; however, it significantly reduces efficiency under the thinking mode. Therefore, there should be an environment variable to serve as the default toggle for thinking. Of course, if thinking-related parameters are included in API requests, those request parameters take precedence. If real data indicates that most users do not need the default thinking mode, the default should be directly changed to "no thinking." If no supporting data exists, introducing a new environment variable is an appropriate solution.

Two images with identical pixel dimensions collapse into one (qwen3.x vision); no error, and the surviving image is unpredictable
When a single request carries two images with identical pixel dimensions, a qwen3.x vision model receives only one of them. `prompt_eval_count` is billed for a single image and the model describes a single image. There is no error and no warning — the response looks normal.
Making the two images differ by one pixel is enough for both to be encoded.
This is not #15147: that one fails loudly with `Internal Server Error -- Failed to create new sequence: SameBatch may not be specified within numKeep` and is fixed by raising `num_ctx`. This one returns HTTP 200 with a confident answer about the wrong image, and `num_ctx` makes no difference (tested at 8192, 16384 and 32768).
It matters because the natural use of two images is comparison — a render against a reference, a before against an after, a photo against a generated image — and pipelines that produce both at the same canonical resolution hit this on every call. The verdict silently describes one image while the caller believes both were seen.

Self-contained, standard library only, no image files needed. It builds two PNGs (red with a horizontal white band, blue with a vertical white band), sends both in one message, then repeats with the second image one pixel narrower:

Both images are encoded and both colours are reported.

`save_as='report.docx'` or `save_as="report.docx"` instead of the canonical

server's warning log, so the client cannot recover or retry intelligently.

2nd or later. `<|"|>` raw-string arguments themselves work.

range). Related: #15241, #15315, #15539, PR #15255, PR #16075.

Bug: Vulkan buffer allocation fails (~900MB-1GB) with a larger prompt, despite >14GB VRAM free
Update: found the actual root cause of this a few days after filing, and it wasn't the Vulkan allocator itself — it was an environment variable silently forcing us onto Vulkan in the first place.
>
Root cause: `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=-1` was set at the user environment level on this machine (origin unknown — possibly left over from an earlier install/driver troubleshooting step, we never pinned down exactly when/how). This tells the HIP runtime to expose zero GPUs, so ROCm can never see the card at all — which is exactly what we saw when testing `OLLAMA_LLM_LIBRARY=rocm_v7_1` above (`hipGetDeviceCount failed: 100`). With ROCm blind to the GPU, Ollama falls back to Vulkan, which is where this specific buffer allocation bug lives.
>
Fix: removed the variable (`[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES", $null, "User")` in PowerShell, then restarted). After that, Ollama picks up the RX 9060 XT via native ROCm (confirmed via the server startup log: `library=ROCm compute=gfx1200`, no more Vulkan fallback). A separate tool on this same machine (ComfyUI, also ROCm-based) started recognizing the GPU natively at the same time, which is what made us suspect an environment-level cause rather than something Ollama- or Vulkan-specific.
>
Since switching to ROCm, we haven't seen the Vulkan buffer allocation failure from the original report at all — makes sense, since that failure mode is specific to the Vulkan backend, and we're no longer on it. To be clear about what this do

Summary
When you type a prompt into a chat's composer but don't send it, then navigate to another chat and come back, the typed draft is gone.

2. Click another chat (Chat B) in the sidebar.
3. Click back on Chat A.

convert: parseTorch ignores the supplied fs.FS and resolves paths against the working directory
`parseTorch` receives an `fs.FS` but resolves paths against the process working directory, so converting a PyTorch-format model looks for the weights in the wrong place.
`parseTensors` builds its file list with `fs.Glob(fsys, ...)`, so the names are fs-relative. `parseSafetensors` opens them with `fsys.Open(p)`. `parseTorch` passes the same relative name to `pytorch.Load(p)`, which uses the OS filesystem. The only production caller is `convert.ConvertModel(os.DirFS(tmpDir), ...)` in `server/create.go`, and the server's working directory is not `tmpDir`.
This covers the `pytorch_model.bin`, `pytorch_model-*-of-*.bin` and `consolidated.*.pth` patterns.
Repro, as a test in `convert`:
dir := t.TempDir()
os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(dir, "pytorch_model.bin"), []byte("not a pickle"), 0o644)
_, err := parseTorch(os.DirFS(dir), strings.NewReplacer(), "pytorch_model.bin")
The content is deliberately invalid, so a pickle error would tell us the file was found. Instead:
open pytorch_model.bin: The system cannot find the file specified.
Go 1.27.0, Windows, against `main` at `ef117cf`. The file exists in `dir`; the working directory was `convert`.
No patch attached because the fix needs a call I would rather leave to you: `gopickle`'s `pytorch.Load` only accepts an OS path, so honouring `fsys` means either copying the tensor file out of the FS, which is expensive for multi-gigabyte weights, or threading the base directory through `ConvertModel`. I can implement whichever you prefer.

MLX runner: fatal OOM at long context — prefix-cache eviction only counts paged-out snapshots, no alloc-failure retry
Summary
On a 64 GB Apple Silicon Mac, the MLX runner dies mid-request (HTTP 500) when a long-context request runs while the prefix cache holds paged-out snapshots from prior requests. The snapshots are within the 8 GiB `maxPagedOutBytes` budget — i.e. eviction is working as designed — but the policy only accounts for paged-out snapshot bytes, never total process memory. During a long prefill there is no eviction trigger, and there is no "Metal allocation failed → evict snapshots → retry" fallback, so the process simply gets killed.
This is a fatal failure mode, distinct from the swap/performance degradation described in #18131 (fixed 8 GiB budget too large on 32 GB) and the benign growth discussed in #17924.

On ollama 0.24.0 (Linux, Fedora, AMD Strix Halo–class UMA APU, runner using the
Vulkan ggml backend — `/usr/local/lib/ollama/vulkan/libggml-vulkan.so`), the runner

threads idle (~13k ticks).

spinning thread inside `libggml-vulkan.so` (Vulkan ggml backend path).

normally, `expires_at` kept advancing — but no `/api/chat`/`/api/generate` request ever

has since run thousands of generations without recurrence.
Why this is nasty operationally
Every health surface that doesn't *generate* stays green: the API answers, the model
lists as loaded, the process is alive. Only an end-to-end generation reveals the wedge.

ollama-cloud: expose per-model metadata in the model API mirroring other providers
Summary
`/api/show` and `/v1/models` currently expose only a boolean `thinking` capability and a `details` block (family, param size, quantization). They do not report, per model:
supported `reasoning_effort` levels,
maximum output-token limit,
context window (only indirectly, via `model_info.*.context_length`),
whether prompt caching applies and at what per-token rate,
per-token pricing (input / output / cache-read).
Clients therefore cannot discover this data programmatically. They must hardcode per-family tables, probe the completion API, or scrape web pages.
Why it matters / who needs it
My very own pi-ollama-cloud Pi extension needs to assemble metadata it cannot fetch to render a proper model list, and currently works around the gaps as follows:

Qwen3-Coder tool parser changes number arguments outside int64 range
The Qwen3-Coder tool parser changes valid `number` arguments outside the `int64` range. For example, a tool call passing `x=1e20` becomes `{"x":9223372036854775807}` on macOS/ARM64, rather than `{"x":100000000000000000000}`. Negative values outside the range are also changed.
`parseTypedToolValue` parses the value as `float64`, then converts every whole-valued float to `int64`. Large finite numbers such as `1e20` have no fractional part but do not fit in `int64`. The conversion loses the original value before the tool call reaches the caller. This can affect scientific/calculation tools with a JSON Schema `number` parameter.
Reproduction
Save the following outside the repository (for example `/tmp/tool-number.go`) and run `go run /tmp/tool-number.go` from the Ollama checkout. This exercises the actual registered parser and JSON serialization without running a model or server.
package main
import (
"encoding/json"
Observed on `53fed26112817f7c55f664efb9e3f65f06cab7db`, Go 1.26.3, macOS/ARM64:
{"x":9223372036854775807}
Expected:
{"x":100000000000000000000}
The precise out-of-range integer conversion result can depend on the architecture; the original number should be preserved regardless.
The narrow fix is to retain the float when it falls outside the `int64` range, while retaining current integer conversion for whole numbers inside that range. The positive boundary needs an exclusive comparison because `float64(math.MaxInt64)` rounds to `1<<63`.

Feature request: yield idle model VRAM under GPU-memory pressure
Summary
Please add an optional, best-effort policy for an idle Ollama model to release its VRAM early when another GPU application needs memory.
Why
The keep-alive timer is useful, but it does not account for a game, video editor, renderer, or other GPU-heavy application starting while a model is still resident but not actively generating. Users currently need to wait for the timer or manually run `ollama stop`.
Desired behavior
Never unload while a request is actively generating or tools are running.
When the runner is idle, detect meaningful GPU-memory pressure and unload the model plus KV cache before the keep-alive timer expires.
Reload automatically on the next request, accepting the normal cold-start delay.
Make it opt-in and configurable, with clear logs when a pressure-driven unload occurs.
This should be best-effort because GPU-memory pressure reporting differs across Windows drivers and GPU backends. Even so, proactive cooperation would make local models far easier to share with games and other demanding GPU applications without an out-of-memory failure or manual intervention.
A companion application such as Hermes Desktop could expose this as a friendly “release local model VRAM while idle” setting and treat a resulting unload as expected.

Structured outputs: JSON schema property order lost on the native llama-server chat path (regression of #7978)
When a JSON schema is passed through `response_format` on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, the declared order of object properties is not preserved on the native llama-server chat path: the model is constrained to emit keys in alphabetical order. For step-dependent schemas this changes the output (e.g. a decision field declared first is generated after its dependent fields), which is the problem originally reported in #7978.
Minimal reproduction
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
"model": "<a model without renderer/parser, e.g. a local tag created FROM ornith-1.5:9b>",
"messages": [{"role":"system","content":"Reply with a JSON object only."},
{"role":"user","content":"Give a colour and an animal."}],
Expected: `{"zeta_colour": ..., "alpha_animal": ...}` (declared order).
Actual on 0.35.0: `{"alpha_animal": ..., "zeta_colour": ...}`. The same alphabetical ordering was observed on 0.33.2.
Likely cause
`llm/llama_server.go` (v0.35.0, `llamaServerChatResponseFormat`, lines ~2415-2431) unmarshals the schema into a `map[string]any` and re-marshals it into the llama-server request. `encoding/json` sorts map keys, so llama.cpp receives an alphabetically ordered `properties` object and builds a grammar with that fixed order.
The OpenAI layer itself keeps the schema as `json.RawMessage` (`openai/openai.go`, lines 92 and 762), and the rendered `/completion` path passes it through unchanged (`lsReq.JsonSchema = req.Format`, line 16

[LLM-jp-4] parser for harmony output with a space after special tokens
LLM-jp-4.1 ( also 32b-a3b and 33b) uses the gpt-oss harmony format, but its tokenizer decodes a space after every special token:
<|channel|> analysis<|message|> The user asks ...<|end|><|start|> assistant<|channel|> final<|message|> 日本の首都は東京です。
The `harmony` parser does not recognize `<|channel|> analysis` as a header, so everything ends up in `content` and tool calls are not detected. LLM-jp-4.1 also separates parallel tool calls with `<|end|>` instead of ending each with `<|call|>`. So these models cannot be used with thinking or tools in Ollama.
Proposal
A `llm-jp-4` parser under `model/parsers/`, used with `PARSER llm-jp-4` in a Modelfile. It drops one space after each special token, passes the text to the exported `harmony.HarmonyParser`, and completes a tool call at every `<|end|>`. The `harmony` package is not modified.
Implementation with tests:
Checked on Linux/CUDA with the 8B GGUF: reasoning/content split, single and parallel tool calls, tool result continuation.
llama.cpp handles this format upstream since but Ollama parses llama-server's raw output with its own parsers, so it needs its own.
I can open the PR if this is acceptable.

MLX engine: weights are unwired ~2 s after each request on macOS 27, so the first request after idle pages them back in
On the MLX engine, a loaded model's weights stay wired only while a request is
running. About two seconds after each request macOS releases them, and they
become ordinary pageable memory. On a machine under any memory pressure they are
then compressed or swapped, and the next request waits for them to come back.
This happens with `OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1` and with `load_duration` near zero, so
the model looks loaded the whole time.
The runner means for the weights to stay wired. After the weights load,
`configureWiredMemory` in `mlxrunner/runner.go` sets MLX's wired limit to the
active memory. The limit is set, but on current macOS it does not keep the
memory wired between requests.

Three Ollama instances on the same GPU don't help either.
*Why it matters*: Nimble is text-only and scores answer-token logits (no generation), and its reference serving prefills the context once and scores questions as parallel branches. The qwen35 exclusion (#14510, #4165) was added for multimodal/recurrent-state safety; for a text-only decision model it removes the main benefit of the /v1/systemone design.
*Ask*: allow parallel slots for qwen35 when the model is text-only/decision-type, or add an override to force it; and/or batch the questions of a single /v1/systemone call.

extend `ollama launch` to browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, Brave)
`ollama launch` currently supports CLI/agent integrations and VS Code. I'd like to propose extending it to web browsers — Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera, Brave — so an Ollama model (local at `127.0.0.1:11434` or Ollama Cloud) can power the browser's AI assistant through a session-scoped local bridge.
Browsers are the most-used surface for AI assistance, and running a fully local model behind the browser assistant is exactly the kind of "local agents everywhere" experience Ollama is great at. Community projects (Page Assist, NativeMind) show real demand for browser + Ollama setups, but none of them integrate with `ollama launch`, and each requires its own install dance.
Proposed design
One generic "browser" integration layer in `cmd/launch`, driven by a per-browser profile table rather than five hand-crafted
integrations:
executable path detection per OS (Windows/macOS/Linux),
a per-browser CDP debug port (e.g. unique port per target),
extension delivery strategy per target.
Bridge component (session-scoped, launched alongside the browser): a small local HTTP/CDP driver that
installs/serves the assistant extension,
drives the browser via CDP,
brokers browser-control commands (poll/result queue for the extension),
proxies the assistant's chat/agent traffic to Ollama local or Ollama Cloud.
This is deliberately not baked into `ollama serve` — the model server is always-on, the bridge is session-scoped, and keeping
them separate avoids coupling browser-driving crashes to the model s

Decision models: a basal-1.0 encoding and per-type temperatures for /v1/systemone
Problem
`/v1/systemone` renders every question in one prompt format (or `clef`), but decision models are trained on one prompt format each. basal-1.0 (Apache-2.0; 1.5B and 4.5B typed-decision models specialised in Polish, also English; on Polish decisions it is ahead of the Jev API and eleven open decision models in its technical report) is trained on its own format:
a fixed system prompt per language,
`State / Question / Options` with lettered options,
an assistant turn prefilled with `{"answer": "`,
both option orders averaged,
per-type temperature calibration.
Through Ollama's generic decision prompt, basal-1.0-1.5B loses up to 0.24 accuracy on a 50-item PL/EN triage set (data-class `noul` 0.70 → 0.46, `score` 0.38 → 0.18). Today the only faithful way to run it is its own Python server.
Proposal
A `basal` decision encoding, selected the same way as `clef`: by GGUF metadata ` .decision.type = "basal"`.
Each question becomes two candidate-scoring rows (original and reversed option order) rendered in basal's prompt format. Option texts follow the reference server. Limit: 2–10 options.
`Answer` averages the rows of a question when an encoding scores several orders.
Optional per-type temperatures ` .decision.temperature.{choice,noul,score}` (`p ∝ p^(1/T)`), read from model metadata. This works for any encoding; nothing changes when the metadata is absent.

Summary
On Ollama 0.35.1, `POST /api/generate` accepts a complete JSON request
object followed by non-JSON data.
The request uses `Content-Type: application/json`, but the complete request
body is not a valid JSON document.
For example, appending:
NOT JSON HERE
after an otherwise valid request still returns HTTP 200 and runs generation.
Reproduction
Model:
gemma4:e4b
Request:
curl -sS -i http://localhost:11434/api/generate \
-H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--data-binary '{"model":"gemma4:e4b","prompt":"Say hi.","stream":false,"options":{"num_predict":8}} NOT JSON HERE'
The complete request body is:
{"model":"gemma4:e4b","prompt":"Say hi.","stream":false,"options":{"num_predict":8}} NOT JSON HERE
The body is not valid JSON because non-whitespace data follows the completed
top-level JSON object.
For comparison, Python's `json.loads()` rejects the complete body with an

Expected behavior
The malformed request should be rejected with HTTP 400 rather than starting
generation.
A JSON error response indicating that the request body is invalid would allow
clients to detect request-serialization mistakes.
Actual behavior
Ollama accepts the malformed request with HTTP 200 and performs generation.
Across three repetitions, all three trailing-garbage requests were accepted
and returned generated text.

`done_reason:"stop"` or at the configured `num_predict` limit with

always shows cached = 0, even though Ollama Cloud's backend prompt cache
